topic: the Pythagorean theorem converse (identifying right triangles)

easy.text: If a triangle's three sides satisfy a² + b² = c², what type of triangle must it be?

options.text: A right triangle
options.feedback: Correct -- this relationship is only true for right triangles.

options.text: An equilateral triangle
options.feedback: Equilateral triangles have all equal sides and angles, which isn't guaranteed by this equation.

options.text: An obtuse triangle
options.feedback: Obtuse triangles don't satisfy this exact equation -- their longest side squared is actually greater than the sum of the other two squared.

options.text: A triangle with no sides at all
options.feedback: This equation confirms a specific type of triangle exists, not that no triangle exists.

medium.text: A triangle has sides of 5, 12, and 13. Is this a right triangle?

options.feedback: Correct -- since the Pythagorean relationship holds true, this must be a right triangle.

options.text: No, because the sides don't form a valid triangle
options.feedback: These sides do form a valid triangle -- in fact, they satisfy the exact right-triangle relationship.

options.text: Yes, because all three sides are different lengths
options.feedback: Having three different side lengths alone doesn't guarantee a right triangle -- the specific Pythagorean relationship must hold.

options.text: No, because 5+12 does not equal 13
options.feedback: Simple addition of sides isn't the right test -- the Pythagorean relationship uses squares, not simple addition.

hard.text: A triangle has sides of 7, 8, and 10. Is this triangle a right triangle?

options.text: No, because 7²+8²=113, which does not equal 10²=100
options.feedback: Correct -- since the sums don't match, this triangle does not satisfy the Pythagorean relationship and isn't a right triangle.

options.text: Yes, because 7+8 is greater than 10
options.feedback: This only confirms the sides can form SOME triangle (triangle inequality) -- it doesn't test for a right angle specifically.

options.text: Yes, because all sides are whole numbers
options.feedback: Being whole numbers doesn't determine whether a triangle is a right triangle -- the Pythagorean relationship must specifically hold.

options.text: No, because the triangle is too large
options.feedback: Size isn't the deciding factor -- whether the squared side relationship holds true is what matters.

easy.hard: This special relationship between squared side lengths only holds true for one particular kind of triangle.
easy.medium: This equation is the defining relationship for one very specific triangle type.
easy.easy: This equation only works for right triangles.

medium.hard: Square the two shorter sides, add them together, and compare that sum to the square of the longest side.
medium.medium: Square 5 and 12, add them together, then compare to 13 squared.
medium.easy: Square 5 and 12, add them, and see if it equals 13 squared (169).

hard.hard: Square the two shorter sides, add them together, and compare that sum to the square of the longest side to test for a right angle.
hard.medium: Square 7 and 8, add them together, then compare to 10 squared (100).
hard.easy: Square 7 and 8, add them (113), and compare to 10 squared (100) -- they don't match.

options.feedback: Correct -- 2/3 is approximately 0.667, which rounds to 0.67, added to 5.

medium.easy: Three-fourths as a decimal is 0.75 -- add that to 3.

topic: finding the mode in a frequency table

easy.text: A survey shows 3 people like red, 7 like blue, and 2 like green. What is the mode of this data?

options.text: Blue
options.feedback: Correct -- blue has the highest frequency (7), making it the mode.

options.text: Red
options.feedback: Red only has a frequency of 3, less than blue's 7.

options.text: Green
options.feedback: Green only has a frequency of 2, the lowest of the three.
This is the total number of people surveyed, not the mode (most frequent category).

medium.text: In a class, test scores show: 70 (4 students), 80 (6 students), 90 (6 students), 100 (2 students). What can you say about the mode?

options.text: There are two modes: 80 and 90, since both have the highest frequency of 6
options.feedback: Correct -- when two values are tied for the highest frequency, the data set is called bimodal, with two modes.

options.text: The mode is 100, since it's the highest score
options.feedback: The mode is about frequency (how often a value appears), not the numerical value itself -- 100 only appears twice.

options.text: The mode is 70, since it's the lowest score
options.feedback: The mode is about frequency, not the lowest value -- 70 only appears 4 times, fewer than 80 or 90.

options.text: There is no mode in this data set
options.feedback: There actually are two tied modes here (80 and 90), not zero.

hard.text: A data set has every single value appearing exactly once (no repeats at all). What can be said about its mode?

options.text: The data set has no mode, since no value repeats more often than any other
options.feedback: Correct -- mode requires at least one value to occur more frequently than others; with no repeats, there's no clear "most common" value.

options.text: The mode is the largest number in the set
options.feedback: Mode isn't about the largest value -- it's about the most frequently occurring value, which doesn't exist here since nothing repeats.

options.text: The mode is the smallest number in the set
options.feedback: Mode isn't about the smallest value -- it's about frequency, which is equal (1) for every value here.

options.text: Every single number in the set is automatically a mode
options.feedback: By convention, if no value repeats more than any other, the data set is typically described as having no mode at all.

easy.hard: This measure identifies the category or value occurring with the greatest frequency.
easy.medium: This is the value or category that appears the most often.
easy.easy: This is the color that the most people chose.

medium.hard: When multiple values tie for the highest frequency count, all of them qualify as modes simultaneously.
medium.medium: When two scores tie for showing up the most, both of them count as modes.
medium.easy: Since both 80 and 90 show up 6 times each, they're tied for the mode.

hard.hard: The mode requires a value to appear MORE frequently than the others; uniform single occurrence across all values means no value stands out as most frequent.
hard.medium: Since every value appears the same number of times (once), none of them stands out as more frequent than the rest.
hard.easy: Since every value shows up just once, none of them is more common than any other.

topic: calculating simple probability of a compound event with a spinner and coin

easy.text: A coin is flipped once. What is the probability of getting tails?

options.feedback: Correct -- there are two equally likely outcomes, and tails is one of them.
A coin only has two sides, not four possible outcomes.
This would mean tails is guaranteed, which isn't true.
This would mean tails is impossible, which isn't true.

medium.text: A spinner has 4 equal sections numbered 1-4. What is the probability of spinning an even number?

options.feedback: Correct -- 2 out of 4 numbers (2 and 4) are even, giving 2/4=1/2.
This undercounts the even numbers -- there are two (2 and 4), not one.
This is technically correct before simplifying, but should be reduced to 1/2.
This overcounts the even numbers on the spinner -- there are only 2 out of 4.

hard.text: A coin is flipped and a 4-section spinner (numbered 1-4) is spun. What is the probability of getting heads AND spinning an even number?

options.feedback: Correct -- multiply the individual probabilities: 1/2 (heads) × 1/2 (even number) = 1/4.
This only reflects one of the two individual events, not their combined probability.
This doesn't match correctly multiplying 1/2 by 1/2.
This doesn't correctly compute the combined probability of both independent events.

easy.hard: There are only two equally likely outcomes for a coin flip.
easy.medium: Out of two equally likely outcomes, count how many are tails.
easy.easy: A coin has two sides -- what's the chance of one specific side?

medium.hard: Count the favorable outcomes (even numbers) out of the total equally likely outcomes.
medium.medium: Count how many of the 4 numbers are even, then put that over 4.
medium.easy: Two of the four numbers (2 and 4) are even -- put that over 4.

hard.hard: For two independent events happening together, multiply their individual probabilities.
hard.medium: Multiply the probability of heads by the probability of spinning an even number.
hard.easy: Multiply 1/2 by 1/2 to get the combined probability.

easy.text: A table shows: when x=1, y=3; when x=2, y=6; when x=3, y=9. Is this relationship proportional?

options.text: Yes, because y is always 3 times x
options.feedback: Correct -- a constant ratio between y and x (here, always 3) indicates a proportional relationship.

options.text: No, because x and y are different numbers
options.feedback: x and y being different numbers doesn't rule out proportionality -- what matters is whether their ratio stays constant.

options.text: No, because the numbers keep increasing
options.feedback: Increasing values don't rule out proportionality -- what matters is whether the ratio between them stays the same.

options.text: Yes, because all the numbers are odd
options.feedback: Whether numbers are odd or even has nothing to do with proportionality -- the constant ratio is what matters.

medium.text: A table shows: when x=2, y=5; when x=4, y=9; when x=6, y=13. Is this relationship proportional?

options.text: No, because the ratio of y to x is not constant (5/2 ≠ 9/4)
options.feedback: Correct -- proportional relationships require a constant ratio between corresponding values, which isn't the case here.

options.text: Yes, because y increases as x increases
options.feedback: Both values increasing together isn't enough -- the ratio between them must stay exactly constant for true proportionality.

options.text: Yes, because the numbers are all whole numbers
options.feedback: Being whole numbers doesn't determine proportionality -- a constant ratio is required.

options.text: No, because x and y start with different numbers
options.feedback: Starting values being different doesn't determine proportionality -- what matters is whether the ratio stays constant across all points.

hard.text: A relationship is represented by the equation y = 4x + 2. Is this a proportional relationship? Why or why not?

options.text: No, because it has a y-intercept of 2, meaning y isn't zero when x is zero
options.feedback: Correct -- true proportional relationships must pass through the origin (0,0), meaning y=0 when x=0, which fails here.

options.text: Yes, because it includes an x term with a coefficient
options.feedback: Having an x term alone doesn't guarantee proportionality -- the equation must also have no constant added (a y-intercept of 0).

options.text: Yes, because the equation is linear
options.feedback: Being a straight line (linear) is necessary but not sufficient -- it must also pass through the origin to be truly proportional.

options.text: No, because the coefficient 4 is too large
options.feedback: The size of the coefficient doesn't determine proportionality -- the presence of a nonzero y-intercept does.

easy.hard: A proportional relationship maintains one single, unchanging ratio between the two variables throughout.
easy.medium: Check whether dividing y by x gives the same number every single time.
easy.easy: Divide each y by its matching x -- if you always get the same number, it's proportional.

medium.hard: Calculate the ratio of y to x for each pair of values and check whether they all match exactly.
medium.medium: Divide each y-value by its matching x-value and compare the results.
medium.easy: Divide 5 by 2, then 9 by 4 -- do you get the same number both times?

hard.hard: A proportional relationship must be expressible as y=kx with no added constant, meaning it always passes through the point (0,0).
hard.medium: For a relationship to be truly proportional, it needs to pass through the point where both x and y are zero.
hard.easy: Check what happens when x is 0 -- for a proportional relationship, y should also be 0 there.
